notes:
I've gathered extensive material from Enduring Word (Guzik), Gill's Exposition, Ellicott's Commentary, the Pulpit Commentary, Spurgeon's sermons, and the Cambridge Bible. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes.

---

# Proverbs 27 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary

## v. 1 — Do not boast about tomorrow, for you do not know what a day may bring.

**Traditional Reading:** The verse forbids arrogant presumption about the future. It does not forbid wise planning, only an overconfident sense of ability to control tomorrow. James 4:13–16 applies this same principle on the higher ground of submission to God's will. Both boasting about tomorrow and excessive anxiety about it (Mt 6:34) stem from the same root: too much dependence on self rather than on God.

- Enduring Word (Guzik): "It is human nature to be overly confident in what future days hold … The verse is not ruling out wise planning for the future, only one's overconfident sense of ability to control the future" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Ellicott: "This temper of mind, as well as the opposite one of too great anxiety for the morrow (Matthew 6:34), proceed from the same cause, too much dependence upon self" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- Gill: Expounds that no one can be certain of a tomorrow — life is as a vapour, and boasting of future plans in business, charity, or repentance is foolish. "Time is like a teeming woman … big with something; but what that is is not known till brought forth" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Spurgeon (sermon No. 94): Acknowledged the blessing of not knowing the future: "To know the good might lead us to presumption, to know the evil might tempt us to despair. Happy for us is it that our eyes cannot penetrate the thick veil which God hangs between us and tomorrow" – cited at https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/ ; full sermon at https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/proverbs/proverbs.xxxiv.html
- Pulpit Commentary: Notes that classical authors echoed this (Horace, Euripides, Seneca) and links to Christ's parable of the rich fool (Lk 12) – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 2 — Let another praise you, and not your own mouth — a stranger, and not your own lips.

**Traditional Reading:** Self-promotion is distasteful and ineffective; praise from an outsider, even a stranger, carries far more weight. Modern technology multiplies opportunities for self-praise, but the principle remains. The German proverb quoted by Waltke captures it: "Self-praise stinks, friend's praise limps, stranger's praise rings."

- Enduring Word (Guzik): "Honor means much more when it comes from an outside source, even a stranger" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill: Notes exceptions where self-commendation is warranted — as with Samuel (1 Sam 12:3) and Paul (2 Cor 10:18) — when the glory of God or the cause of truth requires it – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Cites John 8:54 ("If I honour myself, my honour is nothing") and the classical maxim "In ore proprio laus sordet" (self-praise is foul) – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 3 — A stone is heavy and sand is a burden, but aggravation from a fool outweighs them both.

**Traditional Reading:** The weight of stone and sand are self-evident physical truths, but the wrath of a fool — the headstrong person who rejects God's wisdom — is a heavier burden to bear than both. The fool's anger cannot be removed; it rests in his bosom and is sometimes intolerable even to himself (as Nabal died under it).

- Enduring Word: "When a fool … expresses their anger and wrath, it is a weighty, dangerous thing" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill: Illustrates with the stone at Laban's well, the burdensome stone of Jerusalem (Zech 12:3), and the stone at Christ's tomb. The fool's wrath "cannot be removed, it rests in his bosom; it is sometimes intolerable to himself; he sinks and dies under the weight of it, as Nabal did" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Ellicott: The fool (Hebrew *evil*) is "the headstrong, self-willed person who has never learned to control himself, but bursts out into the maddest rage when crossed" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 4 — Wrath is cruel and anger is like a flood, but who can withstand jealousy?

**Traditional Reading:** Wrath and anger are open and violent, like a flood that sweeps everything away. But jealousy (*envy* or *jealousy*) is even worse — it is secret, unreasonable, brooding, and never fully subsides. Anger may pass; jealousy abides and works insidiously. It was envy that motivated the religious leaders to arrange Jesus's death (Mt 27:18).

- Enduring Word (Guzik): Cites Kidner — jealousy in Scripture is usually positive (God's jealousy *for* us) but this passage acknowledges the dark side: jealousy *of* rather than *for*. Also cites Poole: envy "is more unjust and unreasonable, as not caused by any provocation … and … more secret and undiscernible, and therefore the mischievous effects of it are hardly avoidable" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill: "An envious man is worse than an angry and wrathful man; his wrath and anger may be soon over … but envy continues and abides, and works insensibly." Traces it to the devil's envy (Wisdom 2:24), Cain's envy of Abel, and the Jews' envy of Christ – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Interprets "envy" particularly as outraged jealousy in the husband-wife relation (cf. Prov 6:34; Song 8:6): "Such jealousy does not blaze forth in some sudden outbreak, and then die away; it lives and broods and feeds itself hourly with fresh aliment" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- Ellicott: "Wrath and anger rage for a while like a storm, and then subside; but jealousy can never be completely set at rest" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm

**Tradition note:** Pentecostal/charismatic commentator David Guzik (Enduring Word) stresses the spiritual dimension — jealousy as a "raging emotion that defies reason … like a consuming fire" (quoting Ross) and notes it was what drove the crucifixion plot. The Reformed-leaning Pulpit Commentary ties it more to marital jealousy. This is a difference of emphasis, not doctrine.

## v. 5 — Better an open rebuke than love that is concealed.

**Traditional Reading:** Love that never expresses itself in deeds, especially the courage to rebuke when needed, is inferior to honest, open rebuke. Hidden love does little good. The rebuke must be kindly, considerate, and prayerfully administered — but it must be given. To withhold rebuke out of fear of offending is not love but a form of hatred (Lev 19:17).

- Enduring Word (Guzik): Quotes Bridges: "Rebuke — kindly, considerately, and prayerfully administered — cements friendship rather than weakens it." Also G. Campbell Morgan: "We do not really like rebuke … our dislike of rebuke leads us to think that those who love us serve us well when they are silent" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill: Clarifies this is not about public rebuke (Mt 18:15 directs private reproof) but reproof "given faithfully and plainly, with openness of heart, and without mincing the matter" — as Paul withstood Peter to his face (Gal 2:11) – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Cites Cicero, Plautus, and Publilius Syrus on the classical understanding that true friendship requires honest correction. "To hold back blame … is to hold back love" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- Desiring God (Baptist/Reformed): "A good Christian friend will point out spiritual things to us we can't see … They will show us areas in our life where we lack joy in God … A Christian friend won't tell us what we want to hear, but what we need to hear" – https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/faithful-are-the-wounds-of-a-friend

## v. 6 — The wounds of a friend are faithful, but the kisses of an enemy are deceitful.

**Traditional Reading:** A true friend's corrective words may hurt (like wounds), but they flow from faithfulness and are designed for healing. The "kisses" of an enemy — flattery and false affection — are deceitful and should be deprecated. Examples include Joab's kiss to Amasa and Judas's kiss to Christ.

- Enduring Word (Guzik): Quotes Waltke — the wounds are "a metaphor for the painful and plain words that must be spoken in a true friendship in order to heal." Also cites Trapp on the enemy's kisses: "Such as were the kisses of Joab, Judas, Absalom, and Ahithophel are not to be fancied, but deprecated and detested" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill: "Friendly reproofs … though they may be severe … proceeding from a spirit of love, faithfulness, and integrity, and designed for the good of the person reproved, ought to be kindly received" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Spurgeon: "The first they ever knew of Jesus was in the character of a faithful friend wounding us for sin … The Roman Emperor conferred freedom on a slave by striking him on the ear: and Jesus sets us free by a blow upon our heart" – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/proverbs-27.html
- Desiring God: Cites Spurgeon further: "True friends put enough trust in you to tell you openly of your faults. Give me for a friend the man who will speak honestly of me before my face" – https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/faithful-are-the-wounds-of-a-friend
- Pulpit Commentary: Notes the Hebrew verb translated "deceitful" (*עתר*) can mean "abundant, profuse" — an enemy is lavish with kisses to hide hatred. "Non omnis qui parcit amicus est, neque omnis qui verberat, inimicus" (Augustine: not everyone who spares is a friend, nor everyone who strikes an enemy) – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 7 — The soul that is full loathes honey, but to a hungry soul, any bitter thing is sweet.

**Traditional Reading:** Over-indulgence produces satiety and contempt even for the finest things (honey), while genuine hunger makes even bitter food delightful. The proverb applies materially, but also spiritually: those satiated with worldly things loathe what is truly sweet (God's word, the Gospel), while those who are spiritually hungry devour it eagerly.

- Enduring Word: Spiritually in the negative sense (Bridges): "May not satiety be as great a curse as famine? Is it not fearfully written on many a professing Christian, he who is full loathes honey?" And in the positive sense (Meyer): "The best way of combating worldliness is by satisfying the heart with something better … Fill your heart with God and His sacred truth, and the things of the world will lose their charm" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Spurgeon (sermon on Prov 27:7): Preached that Christ is in Himself sweeter than the honeycomb, yet there are those who loathe even Him; but to the hungry soul, every bitter thing — even the preaching of the cross — is sweet. "Sweet is liberty to the captive … sweet is pardon to the condemned … sweet is health to the sick, and Jesus is the great physician of souls" – https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/proverbs/proverbs.xxxix.html
- Gill: Applies it to the self-sufficient man "full of his own wisdom … who loathes the Gospel, comparable to the honeycomb for its sweetness" versus the hungry sinner to whom "every bitter thing is sweet" — even the preaching of the cross, doctrines of election, and imputed righteousness – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Ellicott: "In spiritual things, the less we content ourselves with, the less hunger we feel, and less enjoyment do we derive from them" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 8 — Like a bird that strays from its nest is a man who wanders from his home.

**Traditional Reading:** A bird away from its nest is exposed to danger, discomfort, and lack of security. Similarly, a person who wanders from his appointed place — his home, calling, or spiritual community — is vulnerable and out of his element. The proverb indirectly encourages contentment with one's God-given place.

- Enduring Word: "We have a place appointed by God, and we can be as out of place as a bird without a nest if we wander from it." Spurgeon applied it to Christians who wander from church to church: "Too many in our London churches are a sort of flying camp … a set of gipsy-Christians" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Pulpit Commentary: "The proverb indirectly inculcates love of one's home and one's native land." To be a fugitive and vagabond was a terrible punishment (Gen 4:12). The LXX reads it as a man "brought into bondage when he is banished from his own place" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- Gill: Applies negatively to those who "abide not in the calling whereunto they are called" and "wander from the way of spiritual understanding, from the place of divine worship, from the word, ordinances, and commandments of the Lord" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Ellicott: "That wandereth forth as an exile that has lost his home." For the spiritual sense, compares Luke 15:13 (the prodigal) – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 9 — Oil and incense bring joy to the heart, and the sweetness of a friend is counsel to the soul.

**Traditional Reading:** Just as fragrant ointments and perfumes delight the senses, so the wise, heartfelt counsel of a true friend brings joy and wellbeing to the soul. Some renderings suggest that a friend's sweet counsel is even better than one's own private counsel.

- Enduring Word (Guzik): "The gladdening oil and incense is a simile for the agreeable and delightful counsel of a friend that originates in his very being" (Waltke). The proverb should prompt the question: "Is there someone in my life who can give hearty counsel?" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Pulpit Commentary: Explains the cultural background — ointments, perfumes, and incense were used at entertainments to honour guests (cf. Prov 7:16–17; Dan 2:46). The friend's words are "sweet and loving words of one who speaks from the depths of his soul" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- Gill: Notes the alternative Jewish reading: "the sweetness of a man's friend, more than the counsel of his soul" — meaning a friend's counsel surpasses one's own. Applies it to Christ's counsel: "to buy of him gold tried in the fire, white raiment, eye salve" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 10 — Do not forsake your friend or your father's friend … better a neighbor nearby than a brother far away.

**Traditional Reading:** Longstanding friendships — especially hereditary ones — are to be cherished and not abandoned. In a day of calamity, the tried friend may be more reliable than even a blood brother. The phrase "near" and "far off" can refer to physical proximity (the neighbour on the spot helps immediately) or emotional closeness. Solomon himself exemplified this by maintaining friendship with Hiram, his father David's friend (1 Kgs 5:1–10), while Rehoboam's rejection of his father's counsellors cost him the kingdom (1 Kgs 12:6–19).

- Enduring Word: "We should hold the bonds of friendship as dear and obligating, even beyond generations." Notes Garrett: the verse is "surprising for appearing to go against custom" because normally Israelites would turn to relatives – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill: Jarchi interprets this of God, "the friend of Israel and of their fathers, who is not to be forsaken." The phrase about the cloudy day means a day of poverty when "former friends care not to come nigh him" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Points out that polygamy weakened brotherly ties — "there was little love between David's sons; and Jonathan was far dearer to David himself than any of his numerous brothers" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- Spurgeon (cited at Enduring Word): "Inasmuch as the Lord Jesus is 'thine own friend, and thy father's friend,' the injunction of the text comes to thee with peculiar force: 'Forsake him not'" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/

## v. 11 — Be wise, my son, and bring joy to my heart, so that I can answer him who taunts me.

**Traditional Reading:** A father (or teacher) exhorts his son to wisdom because a wise son brings gladness and also vindicates the parent against critics. A foolish child brings reproach on the parents, as if they failed in upbringing. The Christian application is that believers' lives should reflect well on their heavenly Father (Mt 5:16).

- Enduring Word: "In some way, the son who rejects wisdom makes the parents look bad … his son will either publicly disgrace the father or enable him to stand proudly before even his enemies" (Garrett) – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Ellicott: "So Christians are exhorted to let their 'light so shine before men' that their Father in heaven may be thereby glorified (Matthew 5:16)" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: "The evil doings of Hebrews often made the Name of God to be blasphemed among the Gentiles; just as nowadays the inconsistent lives of Christians are the greatest impediment to the success of missionary efforts" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 12 — The prudent see danger and take cover; but the simple keep going and pay the penalty.

**Traditional Reading:** A repetition of Proverbs 22:3, reinforcing the contrast between the prudent who foresee evil and hide, and the simple (naïve, untrained in wisdom) who blindly continue and suffer. Spiritually, it describes those who see the evil of sin and flee to Christ versus those who rush headlong into destruction.

- Enduring Word: "Those who are naïve and untrained in wisdom are blind to the potential danger around them." Bridges: "The simple rush blindfolded into hell. The ox has to be driven to destruction, but the sinner plunges into it in spite of every effort to restrain him" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill (spiritual application): The prudent man sees the evil of sin and its punishment, "and hideth himself … in Christ, who is the city of refuge, the stronghold, the rock." The simple "go on in their sinful course of life without any care or concern … till their feet stumble on the dark mountains of eternity" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 13 — Take the garment of him who posts security for a stranger; get collateral if it is for a foreigner.

**Traditional Reading:** A repeated proverb (cf. 20:16). If someone is foolish enough to guarantee the debt of a stranger or a "strange woman" (seductress/foreigner), they are a bad credit risk — demand collateral. It is a practical warning against entangling oneself financially with untrustworthy people.

- Enduring Word: "The man is as immoral and foolish to be surety for a seductress, then we should especially regard them as a credit risk" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Gill: Refers to his comments on Proverbs 20:16, where he treats it as a warning against rash suretyship – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 14 — If one blesses his neighbor with a loud voice early in the morning, it will be counted to him as a curse.

**Traditional Reading:** Excessive, loud, and inappropriately timed praise betrays insincerity and a hidden agenda. The person who begins early in the morning with loud flattery is trying to be first among competitors for the patron's favour. Such profuse protestations of friendship arouse suspicion rather than goodwill, and are received as a curse would be.

- Enduring Word: "His unnatural voice and timing betrays him as a hypocrite and no good will come of it" (Waltke). Trapp: "that extols a man above measure … as the false prophets did Ahab, and the people Herod" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Pulpit Commentary: Compares to Juvenal's satires on parasitic flattery. "The receiver of this sordid adulation, and indeed all the bystanders, would just as soon be cursed by the parasite as blessed in this offensive manner" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- Ellicott: "If gratitude is to be acceptable, the time, place, and manner of shewing it must all be well chosen … So God loves heartfelt gratitude offered in secret (comp. Matthew 6:5-6)" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- Gill: Notes that rising early "lest any should be before him" shows the self-serving motive, and that such a one should be engaged in prayer to God rather than flattery of men – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/proverbs/27.htm

## vv. 15–16 — A constant dripping on a rainy day and a contentious woman are alike — restraining her is like holding back the wind or grasping oil …

**Traditional Reading:** A leaky roof on a rainy day is a picture of relentless irritation — and a contentious (quarrelsome) wife is just like that. Trying to restrain or reform her is as futile as trying to catch the wind or hold oil in your hand. The proverb is a warning to men about the misery of a bad marriage and the importance of choosing wisely.

- Enduring Word: "The man takes shelter under the roof of his home expecting to find protection from the storm. Instead, he finds his leaky roof provides him no shelter … Likewise, he married with the expectation of finding good, but the wife … harshly attacks him at home" (Waltke). Then advises: instead of trying to change a contentious woman, a godly husband loves her as Christ loves the church and leaves the changing to God – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Pulpit Commentary: "Whoever tries to restrain a shrewish woman, or to conceal her faults, might as well attempt to confine the wind." Notes the old adage: three things cannot be hidden — a woman, the wind, and ointment – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- Ellicott: "You might as well try and stop the wind from blowing as seek to restrain her. And oil meeteth his right hand — i.e., if he puts out his hand to stop her she slips through it like oil" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 17 — As iron sharpens iron, so one man sharpens another.

**Traditional Reading:** One of the most quoted proverbs on friendship. Just as iron sharpens iron through friction, striking, and sparks, so godly friends improve each other through honest interaction — sometimes involving friction and constructive criticism. The "countenance" (face/personality) of a friend is sharpened, brightened, and improved. "We shouldn't be afraid of the friction that leads to godly sharpening."

- Enduring Word (Guzik): "The analogy infers that the friend persists and does not shy away from critical, constructive criticism" (Waltke). Bridges: "Gladly let us take up the bond of brotherhood. If a brother seems to walk alone, sharpen his iron by godly communication" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Ellicott: "The play of wit with wit sharpens and brightens up the face" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Some (like Aben Ezra) took this in a bad sense — one angry word provokes another — but "the best commentators understand the maxim to say that intercourse with other men influences the manner, appearance, deportment, and character of a man, sharpens his wits, controls his conduct, and brightens his very face" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm
- JFB Commentary: "Conversation promotes intelligence, which the face exhibits" – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/proverbs-27.html

**Tradition Note:** Most Protestant traditions take this verse positively (mutual edification through honest friendship). The older Jewish interpretation (Aben Ezra) as mutual provocation to anger is noted in the Pulpit Commentary but generally rejected in Christian exegesis.

## v. 18 — Whoever tends a fig tree will eat its fruit, and he who looks after his master will be honored.

**Traditional Reading:** Diligent service brings its reward. The fig tree, requiring closer attention than other plants, represents careful tending; the worker deserves to enjoy the fruit of his labour. Applied to serving a master (earthly or heavenly): faithful service will be honoured. Christ promised, "Well done, thou good and faithful servant" (Mt 25:21).

- Enduring Word: "It isn't right to keep honor from the one who has faithfully waited on his master. God promised to reward those who wait upon Him. Do your work diligently and leave promotion and reward up to God" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Spurgeon (sermon "The Way to Honor" on Prov 27:18): Listed ways God honours His servants: We are honoured in our Master's honour, with His approval, by being given more to do, in the eyes of fellow servants, and by the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit – https://ccel.org/ccel/spurgeon/proverbs/proverbs.xxxviii.html
- Pulpit Commentary: "He who pays attention, has loving regard to his master, shall meet with honour as his reward at his master's hands, and also from all who become acquainted with his merits" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 19 — As water reflects the face, so the heart reflects the true man.

**Traditional Reading:** The Hebrew is cryptic: "As the water the face to the face, so the man's heart to the man." Two main interpretations exist: (1) Just as still water mirrors the face, the heart of one man mirrors the heart of another — we see in others what is in ourselves (Ellicott, Cambridge). (2) Just as water shows a face its reflection, so a man's heart reveals what kind of man he truly is — our inner thoughts, loves, and values reveal our true character (Guzik, Constable).

- Enduring Word (Guzik): "The feelings and thoughts that come from our heart reveal us as the reflection in smooth water reveals the face. Who we are will eventually be evident to others" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Ellicott: "What is in our own hearts we find in others also. Whatever are the distinguishing features of our own characters we discover and elicit the same in others. The merciful, the generous, the devout, the pure, recognise the same qualities in others" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- Cambridge Bible: Gives both renderings (R.V. text and margin). The "heart as mirror" reading means: "A sordid nature or ruffled temper, like turbid or unsettled water, will give a broken and distorted image" — we judge others by ourselves. The alternative: the heart reveals a man to another man – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/proverbs/27.htm
- Constable (Evangelical): "If you want to see what a man is really like, look in his heart. That is, find out what he loves and values and you will know what kind of person he is" – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-27.html

## v. 20 — Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.

**Traditional Reading:** The grave and the realm of destruction (Sheol and Abaddon) never say "enough" — they endlessly devour the dead. Similarly, human desire (the "eyes") is never satisfied; lust, greed, and craving are insatiable. The answer is to find satisfaction in God alone (Ps 36:8–9; 1 Cor 2:9).

- Enduring Word: "Our longing to look upon things we desire will never be satisfied; it must be controlled and brought under God's dominion. A man will never see enough alluring images of women or enough beautiful machines" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Ellicott: "God would thus teach us that in Himself only can man find complete satisfaction" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- Trapp (via Enduring Word): "That is, their lusts, their carnal concupiscence. To seek to satisfy it is an endless piece of business" – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/

## v. 21 — A crucible for silver and a furnace for gold, but a man is tested by the praise accorded him.

**Traditional Reading:** Just as the crucible and furnace test and purify precious metals by fire, so praise tests a man's character. How one handles praise reveals what sort of person he is: vain men seek it, weak men are inflated by it, wise men disregard it. Alternatively, the thing a man praises or boasts about reveals his character.

- Ellicott: Three interpretations: (a) what a man boasts about reveals his character; (b) praise/popularity tests a man as fire tests metal — only good metal comes through unharmed; (c) a man should test his praise — examine its source and genuineness – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- JFB: "Praise tests character … Thus vain men seek it, weak men are inflated by it, wise men disregard it" – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/proverbs-27.html
- Cambridge Bible: The R.V. reads "a man is tried by his praise" — i.e., by the manner in which he bears praise. Another marginal reading: "that which he praiseth" or "that whereof he boasteth" — you test a man's character by observing what he praises in others or boasts of in himself – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/proverbs/27.htm

## v. 22 — Though you grind a fool like grain with mortar and a pestle, yet his folly will not depart from him.

**Traditional Reading:** Even the most severe treatment — pounding a fool like grain in a mortar — cannot separate him from his folly. Folly has become intrinsic to his nature. Just as pounding separates husk from wheat, violent measures might seem to separate folly from the fool, but his obstinacy is too deep-rooted.

- Ellicott: "This would separate completely the husks from the wheat; but obstinacy has become a part of such a man's nature, and cannot be got rid of even by such violent measures" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- JFB: "The obstinate wickedness of such is incurable by the heaviest inflictions" – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/proverbs-27.html
- Cambridge Bible: Notes the word rendered "wheat" is actually "bruised corn" (as in 2 Sam 17:19) – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/proverbs/27.htm

## vv. 23–27 — Be sure to know the state of your flocks … for riches are not forever … the lambs will provide you with clothing … plenty of goats' milk …

**Traditional Reading:** This closing poem (vv. 23–27) extols the virtues of diligent pastoral stewardship. The principle: know the condition of what God has entrusted to you, supervise it personally, and work hard — because wealth is fleeting and even a crown does not last. Nature's cycles (hay removed, new growth, mountain herbs gathered) provide for the diligent: lambs give clothing, goats can be sold to purchase fields, and goats' milk nourishes the household. The passage shows the interplay between human labour and divine provision.

- Enduring Word: "We should work hard (be diligent) to know the state of whatever God has given us management over. If you don't know the condition of something, you can't effectively manage or lead it." Trapp: "Set thy heart to them … leave not all to servants, though never so faithful; but supervise and oversee business, as Boaz did." Poetical application: "People should preserve what income they have because it does not long endure" (Ross) – https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/
- Ellicott: "In the last five verses of this chapter the peace and security of the pastoral life are described as being far superior to the uncertainty attending other sources of wealth and the regal power. For the spiritual sense of this passage comp. 1 Peter 5:2-4" (shepherding the flock of God) – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/proverbs/27.htm
- JFB: "Flocks constituted the staple of wealth. It is only by care and diligence that the most solid possessions can be perpetuated … The fact that providential arrangements furnish the means of competence to those who properly use them is another motive to diligence" – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/proverbs-27.html
- Constable (Evangelical): Calls this "A Discourse on Prudence" (27:23–27): "The essentials stressed here are the care of one's resources, hard work, and a recognition and appreciation of God's provisions." Notes goat's milk was the animal nutrient of choice in the ancient Near East — "richer in protein and easier to digest than cow's milk" (Waltke) – https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/proverbs-27.html
- Cambridge Bible: "The praises of agriculture, or of pastoral life. It well repays the diligence bestowed upon it (v. 23), and is more reliable in its nature than other kinds of wealth, and even than a kingly crown (v. 24)" – https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/proverbs/27.htm

**Tradition Note on vv. 23–27:** This passage is sometimes cited in "prosperity" or Word of Faith contexts as proof that diligent stewardship of resources inevitably yields material blessing. The traditional commentators, however, stress that the passage describes the general providence of God through natural cycles, not a mechanical guarantee of wealth. The JFB commentary explicitly frames it as "providential arrangements" that "furnish the means of competence to those who properly use them" — meaning God provides through ordinary means, not through a formula of guaranteed return. The older commentators (Ellicott, Cambridge) are careful to point to the spiritual application (1 Pet 5:2–4, shepherding God's flock) as the deeper meaning.

## Summary of Where Protestant Traditions Differ

The search results did not yield explicit verse-by-verse denominational splits on Proverbs 27 from the approved sites for Baptist, Methodist, Lutheran, Anglican, or Pentecostal distinctives. However, several emphases can be noted:

- **Reformed / Baptist (Desiring God, Spurgeon):** Heavy emphasis on vv. 5–6 as describing the nature of sanctifying friendship within the church — friends who exhort one another toward Christ and away from sin. The "wounds" are specifically gospel-centered correction. (https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/faithful-are-the-wounds-of-a-friend)

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / Guzik):** Tends to highlight the spiritual warfare dimension (e.g., jealousy as a "raging emotion … like a consuming fire" driving the crucifixion, v. 4) and the personal, devotional application to the believer's walk. The tone is practical and application-heavy rather than heavily doctrinal. (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-27/)

- **Older classic commentaries (Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Cambridge):** These are broadly used across traditions. Gill (Particular Baptist) applies many proverbs Christologically (e.g., v. 9, v. 10, v. 12). Ellicott (Anglican) and the Pulpit Commentary consistently cross-reference New Testament passages and classical literature. The Cambridge Bible offers textual-critical notes.

- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to retrieve pages from newadvent.org, catholic.com, or oca.org within the search limits. The Catholic view of Proverbs generally follows the same literal and moral readings as Protestant commentators (Proverbs is part of the shared canon), with the possible addition of a spiritual/mystical sense in some verses, but I could not confirm specific differences from the permitted sites.

- **Modern scholarship:** I was unable to retrieve netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org within the fetch limit. The NET Bible notes typically address translation issues and historical context (e.g., the agricultural images in vv. 23–27).
